units.title: Unit 05 — Register
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 14–15 (PDF pages 18–19).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Learning about collocations · context and register
learningObjectives: Identify whether word combinations belong mainly to informal conversation, formal notices, headlines or business contexts.
Understand the typical meanings of concise, dramatic news verbs and replace them with neutral alternatives when appropriate.
Use characteristic business expressions in suitable contexts.
Recognise and produce appropriate register contrasts without assuming literal synonyms share the same style.

items.example: The weather was pretty awful throughout our trip.
items.note: Pretty intensifies a negative adjective in casual spoken English; it is less suitable for a formal report.

items.example: The hotel service was pretty dreadful last weekend.
items.note: An informal way to give a strongly negative assessment; dreadful itself is already emphatic.

items.example: The first half of the lecture was pretty dull.
items.note: In conversation, pretty can mean fairly or quite, not attractive.

items.example: The children were bored stiff during the long delay.
items.note: A vivid informal expression for being extremely bored.

items.pt: estar precisando muito cortar o cabelo
items.example: I badly need a haircut before the interview.
items.note: Badly need means need urgently or very much; it does not describe poor-quality need.

items.pt: precisar muito ser cortado; estar precisando de corte
items.example: Those overgrown bushes badly need cutting before the outdoor event.
items.note: British English often uses need + -ing with a passive meaning: needs cutting means needs to be cut.

items.example: I will have a think before accepting the proposal.
items.note: Common informal British English meaning consider something for a while.

items.pt: me dar uma ligada; me telefonar
items.example: Please give me a ring when you arrive.
items.note: An informal British English alternative to give me a call; ring here means phone.

items.example: Passengers should alight from the bus only at designated stops.
items.note: Alight is a formal word for get off, often seen on transport notices.

items.example: The sign says cyclists must dismount near the bridge.
items.note: Dismount means get off a bicycle or similar vehicle and is common in instructions and signs.

items.example: The notice warns that trespassers will be prosecuted.
items.note: A conventional warning in formal legal notices; trespassers enter property without permission.

items.example: Residents must dispose of unwanted items at the collection point.
items.note: Dispose of is more formal than throw away and normally takes the preposition of.

items.example: Visitors should leave their badges in the receptacle provided near reception.
items.note: Formal signage may use receptacle to mean a container and provided to mean supplied for use.

items.example: We will board the aircraft through the front door.
items.note: Formal travel announcements favour board the aircraft over get on the plane.

items.pt: arcar com o custo dos reparos
items.example: The supplier agreed to bear the cost of repairs.
items.note: Bear the cost of is a formal expression meaning pay for or accept financial responsibility.

items.pt: desistir formalmente de um curso; cancelar matrícula
items.example: She decided to withdraw from a course after the first term.
items.note: More formal than drop out of a course; withdraw emphasises the act of leaving or cancelling participation.

items.example: She embarked upon a detailed explanation of the findings.
items.note: Embark upon is formal and means begin an undertaking, speech or explanation.

items.pt: cortar postos de trabalho; eliminar empregos
items.example: The company may axe jobs after the merger.
items.note: Axe is a short, dramatic headline verb meaning eliminate jobs; less common in ordinary conversation.

items.example: Several retailers plan to slash prices before the holiday.
items.note: Slash suggests a large, rapid reduction and is frequent in headlines.

items.example: Pump prices fell for the second consecutive week.
items.note: A concise news expression for the price of petrol or diesel at filling stations.

items.example: Major oil companies announced changes to fuel prices.
items.note: Major conveys large size or importance, especially in reporting on an industry.

items.example: Experts warned that government spending will rocket after the new measures.
items.note: Rocket is a vivid media verb meaning rise very fast; rise sharply is a more neutral alternative.

items.pt: intensificar a repressão ao excesso de velocidade
items.example: Police will crack down on speeding near schools.
items.note: Crack down on means enforce rules more strictly against an activity.

items.example: Police quiz a suspect after new evidence emerges.
items.note: In headline style, quiz means question or interrogate; ordinary speech would usually say question.

items.example: Detectives identified a prime suspect in the disappearance.
items.note: Prime identifies the main person under investigation, not someone proven guilty.

items.example: A search began for a missing teenager in the area.
items.note: A common concise news phrase for a young person whose whereabouts are unknown.

items.example: A flu outbreak forced the school to cancel the event.
items.note: An outbreak is a sudden rise in cases of an infectious disease.

items.example: Floods hit the region every few years after heavy storms.
items.note: Hit is common in headlines for a damaging event affecting a place.

items.example: Volunteers continue to battle against floods by reinforcing the barriers.
items.note: Battle against is a dramatic expression for making a determined effort against a threat.

items.pt: demitir trabalhadores devido à eliminação de postos
items.example: The factory may make workers redundant if demand falls.
items.note: British English for job losses because roles are no longer required; not the same as dismissal for misconduct.

items.pt: perdas de postos de trabalho; demissões
items.example: The announcement raised fears of further job losses.
items.note: A common media and business noun phrase referring to eliminated jobs.

items.example: Falling profits led the firm to review its costs.
items.note: A financial-reporting combination indicating profits are decreasing.

items.pt: apresentar uma proposta em uma licitação
items.example: Three firms will submit a tender for the construction contract.
items.note: A tender is a formal bid to perform work or supply goods at specified terms.

items.example: The start-up hopes to raise capital from new investors.
items.note: Raise capital means obtain funding for business activity.

items.pt: formar uma sociedade; entrar em parceria comercial
items.example: The designers decided to go into partnership to open a studio.
items.note: A typical business expression for joining forces as partners, often in a venture.

items.pt: abrir uma empresa; iniciar um negócio
items.example: They want to start up a business selling recycled furniture.
items.note: Start up describes creating a new business; start a business is also natural.

items.example: The investment will help us expand the business overseas.
items.note: Expand the business means increase its size, reach or operations.

items.example: The partners hope to develop a range of products for schools.
items.note: Range of products means a related selection of goods sold by a company.

items.example: He is dead keen to join the robotics club.
items.note: Dead is an informal British intensifier, particularly with keen.

items.pt: abandonar a universidade; largar a faculdade
items.example: She did not want to drop out of university after one difficult term.
items.note: Informal for leaving a course or programme before completing it; compare the formal withdraw from.

items.pt: começar a dar uma explicação, de maneira repentina ou longa
items.example: He launched into an explanation before anyone had asked a question.
items.note: Launch into is an expressive, often conversational way to describe beginning to speak at length.

items.pt: demitir trabalhadores por motivos econômicos ou operacionais
items.example: The retailer may lay off workers after several stores close.
items.note: A less headline-like alternative to axe jobs; commonly suggests redundancies or reduced demand.

items.example: The supermarket agreed to reduce prices on basic goods.
items.note: A neutral alternative to the dramatic newspaper collocation slash prices.

sectionsChecked: A · Spoken English and informal intensifiers
sourceAudit.editorialScope: Register-sensitive collocations from spoken, formal, headline and business settings, including key exercise contrasts. Contextual alternatives are included only where they clarify a register choice; incidental words and original exercise text are omitted.

units.title: Unit 06 — Intensifying adverbs
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 16–17 (PDF pages 20–21).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Grammatical aspects of collocations · intensifying adverbs
learningObjectives: Choose highly with its characteristic adjective partners, recognising noteworthy exceptions such as highly controversial.
Combine absolutely or utterly with adjectives of extreme meaning.
Select bitterly, deeply, ridiculously and strongly for idiomatic emotional, evaluative or opinion-related collocations.
Reject unnatural intensifier partnerships while preserving the correct grammar and register of each expression.

items.example: It is highly unlikely that the repairs will finish today.
items.note: Highly strongly intensifies the low probability expressed by unlikely.

items.example: The team is highly likely to meet the deadline.
items.note: Likely and unlikely both combine with highly to express strong probability judgments.

items.example: Such a delay is highly unusual for this service.
items.note: Highly unusual is idiomatic despite unusual not being positive in meaning.

items.example: The charity ran a highly successful fundraising campaign.
items.note: Highly commonly modifies positive evaluations of performance.

items.example: The market for electric vehicles is highly competitive.
items.note: Describes a market or person with intense competition or strong competitive ability.

items.example: The new contract proved highly profitable for the firm.
items.note: Highly intensifies the positive financial quality profitable.

items.example: The new training approach has been highly effective.
items.note: A common expression in professional or academic evaluations.

items.example: The proposal remains highly controversial among residents.
items.note: A noteworthy exception: highly can modify this clearly negative or divisive adjective.

items.example: This introductory handbook is highly recommended for new staff.
items.note: Often used in reviews or recommendations; highly emphasises endorsement.

items.pt: com alto nível de escolaridade; muito instruído
items.example: The workforce is highly educated and technically skilled.
items.note: A valid highly + adjective pairing tested as a contrast with highly exhausted.

items.example: The proposed fee seems absolutely ridiculous to me.
items.note: Absolutely commonly intensifies extreme adjectives such as ridiculous.

items.example: The rumour was utterly ridiculous from the start.
items.note: Utterly gives emphatic, sometimes slightly more formal force to an extreme adjective.

items.example: It would be absolutely stupid to ignore the warning signs.
items.note: An emphatic negative judgement; stupid is already strongly evaluative.

items.example: Leaving the keys in the ignition was utterly stupid.
items.note: The book presents utterly as an intensifier with extreme negative adjectives.

items.example: It is absolutely impossible to complete the test without power.
items.note: Impossible is an absolute adjective that naturally takes absolutely.

items.example: The original schedule became utterly impossible to maintain.
items.note: Utterly emphasises an extreme judgement of impossibility.

items.example: The first calculation was absolutely wrong.
items.note: Absolutely can intensify a clear negative judgement of correctness.

items.example: After everyone left, he felt utterly alone.
items.note: Utterly can make the experience of being alone sound total or emotionally emphatic.

items.example: Parents were utterly appalled by the unsafe conditions.
items.note: Appalled already expresses strong shock or disgust, so utterly is an idiomatic partner.

items.example: I am absolutely convinced that the design can work.
items.note: A fixed intensifier pairing meaning certain beyond reasonable doubt.

items.example: The town was utterly devastated by the storm.
items.note: Utterly strongly intensifies devastated, for physical damage or emotional grief.

items.example: He felt absolutely miserable after the argument.
items.note: An extreme negative emotional judgement; do not confuse miserable with merely a little sad.

items.example: The rescue workers were utterly exhausted by dawn.
items.note: A natural extreme-intensifier pairing; highly exhausted is not idiomatic.

items.example: The idea of cancelling every bus route is absolutely absurd.
items.note: A valid exercise pairing; absurd has a sufficiently extreme meaning for absolutely.

items.example: The residents were utterly opposed to the closure.
items.note: The answer key accepts utterly opposed as well as strongly opposed; use opposed to something.

items.example: We were bitterly disappointed by the cancellation.
items.note: Bitterly commonly intensifies disappointment with a sense of deep sadness or frustration.

items.example: The final result was bitterly disappointing for the players.
items.note: Disappointing describes the event; disappointed describes the people experiencing it.

items.example: I bitterly regret selling my old guitar.
items.note: Often used for serious remorse rather than a minor inconvenience.

items.pt: ressentir-se profundamente de; guardar forte ressentimento
items.example: She bitterly resents being excluded from the meeting.
items.note: Resent normally takes a noun or -ing clause; bitterly signals intense anger or hurt.

items.example: Several reviewers bitterly criticised the decision.
items.note: A particularly forceful criticism, often expressing resentment.

items.example: Local residents complained bitterly about the noise.
items.note: Bitterly can follow complain; it shows strong grievance, not merely a factual complaint.

items.example: She wept bitterly after hearing the news.
items.note: A literary or expressive combination for intense sorrow; less common in ordinary conversation.

items.example: He was deeply ashamed of the way he had behaved.
items.note: Deeply intensifies a strong emotional state, often with ashamed of.

items.example: The engineers are deeply concerned about the safety risk.
items.note: Frequent in formal statements to signal serious worry; concerned about is common.

items.example: The audience was deeply shocked by the discovery.
items.note: Deeply often goes with feelings and emotional responses, not a neutral intensity scale.

items.example: Our colleagues are deeply committed to improving accessibility.
items.note: Commonly followed by to + noun or -ing form; signals lasting dedication.

items.example: I was deeply moved by the students’ farewell speech.
items.note: Moved means emotionally touched; deeply increases the emotional intensity.

items.example: Many families were deeply affected by the flood.
items.note: Can describe emotional or practical impact, often in serious contexts.

items.example: She felt deeply hurt by the accusation.
items.note: This pairing emphasises emotional pain rather than physical injury.

items.example: We deeply regret the inconvenience caused by the cancellation.
items.note: Frequent in formal apologies, letters and announcements.

items.example: The volunteers care deeply about animal welfare.
items.note: With care, the natural unmarked order is care deeply; the book lists deeply with care.

items.example: Her grandparents are deeply religious and attend services regularly.
items.note: Describes strong religious commitment or feeling, not superficial involvement.

items.example: He was deeply unhappy in his previous role.
items.note: A strong, often sustained negative emotional state.

items.example: The last-minute tickets were ridiculously cheap.
items.note: Ridiculously suggests an extreme degree that seems surprising or unreasonable.

items.example: Parking in the city centre has become ridiculously expensive.
items.note: A natural way to criticise a price as unreasonably high.

items.example: The first exercise was ridiculously easy for the class.
items.note: An informal or expressive judgement that the task was much easier than expected.

items.example: The initial offer was ridiculously low.
items.note: Often used for prices, wages, rates or other amounts.

items.example: The monthly service charge was ridiculously high.
items.note: Common for prices, figures, fees and other measured levels.

items.example: The queue was ridiculously long at lunchtime.
items.note: A subjective judgement that a length or duration is excessive.

items.example: The deadline for the assignment was ridiculously short.
items.note: Can refer to duration, length or distance when it seems unreasonable.

items.example: The apartment had a ridiculously small kitchen.
items.note: Combines an extreme evaluation with physical size or amount.

items.example: The machine arrived in a ridiculously large box.
items.note: Suggests a size far beyond what seems necessary.

items.example: They scheduled the meeting for a ridiculously early hour.
items.note: Expresses the speaker’s judgement that a time is unreasonably early.

items.example: Local shop owners strongly oppose the new restrictions.
items.note: A standard strong-opinion combination; oppose is followed directly by its object.

items.example: Family expectations can strongly influence career choices.
items.note: Influence describes an effect on decisions or behaviour; strongly is idiomatic here.

items.example: I strongly believe that public transport should improve.
items.note: A frequent way to signal a firmly held belief.

items.example: The organisation strongly denies the allegations.
items.note: Used for emphatic rejection of a claim or accusation.

items.example: I strongly recommend reading the instructions first.
items.note: A strong recommendation; recommend typically takes a noun or -ing form, not a bare infinitive.

items.example: The committee strongly supports the proposal.
items.note: Expresses clear and emphatic approval of an idea or action.

items.example: The charity strongly condemned the violent attack.
items.note: Common in public statements rejecting an action as unacceptable.

items.pt: sugerir enfaticamente; indicar com muita força
items.example: The findings strongly suggest that the sensor needs recalibration.
items.note: May express advice or strong evidential support; context determines the meaning.

items.pt: sentir com convicção; ter forte opinião
items.example: I strongly feel that we should consult the whole team.
items.note: Frequently followed by a that-clause expressing a firm personal view.

items.pt: argumentar enfaticamente; defender firmemente uma posição
items.example: The researchers strongly argue for more transparent testing procedures.
items.note: Can describe a forcefully defended position in discussion or writing.

items.example: Several residents strongly object to the new road.
items.note: Object is followed by to + noun or -ing, not normally a direct object.

items.example: She strongly dislikes being interrupted while working.
items.note: An idiomatic emphasis on dislike; strongly love is not a normal equivalent.

items.example: Most teachers were strongly opposed to the proposed closure.
items.note: Opposed is commonly followed by to and may take strongly or utterly.

items.example: Access to the test area is strictly forbidden without permission.
items.note: Strictly modifies a prohibition; strongly forbidden is not a natural collocation.

sectionsChecked: A · Highly and its restricted adjective partners
B · Absolutely and utterly with extreme adjectives
C · Bitterly, deeply, ridiculously and strongly
sourceAudit.editorialScope: Representative high-value intensifier pairings from each printed list plus meaningful exercise-only combinations and false-partner contrasts; synonymous intensifier variants are selected for pedagogical value rather than duplicated mechanically.
sourceAudit.exercisePolicy: Original sentences and usage notes; incorrect textbook options appear only as error warnings in notes, never as valid word targets.
